edits.fix: Use the standard footer 'Bellingham Math Circle / Week 1 / <id>' on every page instead of a bare page number at the right margin.

edits.quote: In every problem, blocks go on the lines of the shape.
edits.fix: 'On the lines' can be read as blocks straddling the lines. Say 'Blocks line up with the lines of the shape' (the 2-3 page says 'along its lines').

edits.quote: Build the left picture with blue blocks. Change it into the right picture in as few moves as you can.
edits.fix: The page has three left/right pairs, counting the move example, so say 'For each pair below the example, build the left picture...' so the example is not taken as a task.

edits.quote: For each shape, circle the player who can always win: first or second.
edits.fix: Make 'always win' concrete for K-1 listeners: 'Circle the player who can win every time, no matter how the other player plays.' Answers to check: hexagon second, 6-triangle strip first, 5-triangle trapezoid first.

k-1.summary: A strong K-1 page set. It uses both kernels at an entry level: the six shapes in P1 include three even-area shapes that cannot be covered, P2-P3 ask for the fewest greens (2, 3, 4, 5), P4 asks for every rhombus tiling (2 and 3), P5 has flip puzzles needing 2 and 4 moves, and P6 is a correct Kayles-style game. Boards are actual size and the text is clean. Only small wording fixes remain.

edits.fix: Use the standard footer 'Bellingham Math Circle / Week 1 / <id>' on every page.

edits.quote: Which of these boards can be covered with blue blocks only? Cover each board that you can,
edits.fix: The question repeats the instruction that follows. Keep one: 'Cover each board with blue blocks only and draw where your blocks went. Put an X on each board that cannot be covered.'

edits.quote: Page 2 holds only boards E and F, and page 3 holds only triangles A and B of Problem 2; more than half of each page is blank.
edits.fix: Reflow so actual-size boards fill the pages (for example, put triangle C on page 3). This cuts page flips and paper.

edits.quote: Each board below is a big hexagon with two gray holes, and no block may cover a hole.
edits.fix: The diagrams already show the hexagons and holes. Cut to 'No block may cover a gray hole.' (Checked: A and D can be covered; B has two up-holes and C has two down-holes, so neither can be.)

edits.quote: Could triangle C in Problem 2 be covered with blue blocks and fewer green triangles than you used? Explain.
edits.fix: This is a proof follow-up to P2, and P5's 'Explain how you know' already asks for it. 'Than you used' also makes the answer depend on the child's own count. Delete it, or fold it into P5 ('...for triangles C and D, then for 10 and 100 edges'), and leave the step to the adult.

edits.quote: so that it cannot be covered with blue blocks and fewer than 4 green triangles.
edits.fix: Replace the double negative with a plain statement: 'so that every covering with blue blocks and green triangles needs at least 4 green triangles.'

grades-2-3.summary: This band develops kernel 1 well and every diagram is correct. P1 has three even-area boards that cannot be covered, P3 is a coloring argument on hexagons with holes, P2 and P5 run the fewest-greens sequence (2, 3, 4, 5, then 10 and 100), P6 shows the chevron gives no improvement (purple minimums 4, 5, 4, 5), and P7 asks children to invent a hard board. Edits are light: one redundant proof step, two wording trims, a double negative, and two half-empty pages.

edits.fix: Use the standard footer 'Bellingham Math Circle / Week 1 / <id>' on every page.

edits.quote: The blank small drawings of boards are for recording.
edits.fix: Delete it. Each problem already says where to draw ('draw each way in one of the small copies below'), and the small drawings in P3 are not blank.

edits.quote: Could the first pair in Problem 3 be done in fewer moves than you used?
edits.fix: The answer depends on the child's own count: a child who used 10 moves just answers yes. Ask instead 'What is the fewest number of moves for the first pair in Problem 3? Explain why no fewer will do.' (Answer: 8, since each chain needs 4 swaps. Round trips of 5 or 7 moves are impossible by parity.)

edits.quote: If you run out of copies, you can draw more on the back.
edits.fix: The board has sides 1-3-3 and 20 coverings, but only 4 copies are printed. The pages are single-sided with blank backs, so children cannot redraw triangular-grid hexagons. Add a page of about 20 small copies (or a triangle-grid page) and delete the sentence.

edits.quote: If you run out of copies, you can draw more on the back.
edits.fix: The big hexagon has 20 coverings but only 16 copies are printed. Add at least 4 more (they can share the extra page added for P9) and delete the sentence.

grades-4-5.summary: An excellent development of kernel 2, and every diagram checks out. The 6 tilings and their flip graph come first, the flip puzzles are correct at 8 moves (the maximum) and 4 moves, and round trips work for 4 and 6 moves but not for 5 or 7. The example chain RLLR and all eight chain words for A-D are correct, two of the four chain pairs in P6 are possible and two are not, and the counting problems for the 1-3-3 board and the big hexagon (20 each) close the set. The main fix is recording space for P9 and P10, plus one ambiguous 'than you used'.

overall.strongest: Every board, worked example and expected answer checks out, and each band follows its kernel through a well-chosen, concrete sequence written in plain text with nothing decorative.
overall.weakest: The 4-5 counting problems ask for 20 coverings but print only 4 and 16 copies and send children to the blank backs of single-sided pages; footers also lack the standard id.
